content: Soy allergy is a specific type of food allergy that occurs when the immune system reacts abnormally to soy protein. It is one of the most prevalent food allergies globally. According to the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, soy is classified as one of the nine most common food allergens affecting both children and adults with food allergies. Diagnosis: History and Symptoms Soy allergy can present with symptoms such as urticaria (hives), skin rash, redness caused by inflammation due to an immune response, and intense itching of the skin. These symptoms may appear immediately after consuming soy protein but can also manifest hours or even days later. Treatment: Medical Therapy The primary treatment for soy allergy involves adhering to an exclusion diet, which requires the complete avoidance of foods containing soy or those that may be contaminated with soy ingredients. The most severe reaction to a food allergen, including soy, is anaphylaxis. This is a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate intervention. Treatment for anaphylaxis involves the administration of epinephrine, typically via an autoinjector such as an EpiPen. In some cases, antihistamines like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) may also be administered to manage symptoms. Individuals with soy allergy who experience anaphylaxis may go into anaphylactic shock, a critical condition that demands urgent medical attention. If an allergic reaction occurs, the affected individual should seek immediate medical care by visiting a physician or going to the emergency room, as untreated anaphylaxis can be fatal. Primary Prevention To prevent allergic reactions, individuals with soy allergy must carefully read food ingredient labels and avoid any products containing soybeans or soy-derived substances. Special caution is advised when dining at Asian restaurants or using Asian sauces, as these often contain soy.
